title: Custom BLDC Robot Joint
tools: STM32 · Embedded C · FOC · Onshape · 3D Printing
description: I’m building a compact BLDC actuator from the motor control up, with a focus on making the electronics, firmware, and mechanical design work together.
overview: This is an ongoing personal project to design and build my own robotic joint. I wanted to get beyond using off-the-shelf servos and understand what goes into a robot actuator: controlling a BLDC motor, measuring position, designing a reduction, and eventually integrating everything into one assembly. I’ve been working through the electronics, firmware, and mechanical pieces in parallel, and there’s still a lot to finish.
technical: On the motor control side, I’ve been working with an STM32-based controller and field-oriented control (FOC). I have a working demonstration where the motor follows a potentiometer position and returns to its commanded position after I move it by hand. I’ve also experimented with building a basic three-phase driver using IR2101 gate drivers and six MOSFETs, first on perfboard and then in a more developed soldered prototype. For the mechanical side, I’ve designed and printed different reducer concepts, including planetary and simplified harmonic-style gearboxes, and I’m currently working on a cycloidal reducer in Onshape. The goal is to bring those pieces together into a compact joint.
decisions: I’m deliberately using an off-the-shelf motor controller for the current joint instead of presenting a custom PCB as something I’ve already built. That lets me develop and test the control and mechanical systems without waiting on another board revision. I’ve also been exploring 3D-printed gearboxes because they’re cheap to prototype and make it easy to compare different approaches to reduction and backlash. The cycloidal design is my current direction, but it’s still being developed.
challenges: Getting a BLDC motor to move is one thing; making it behave like a controlled joint is much more interesting. The working position-control demo has been an important milestone, but the full actuator isn’t assembled or validated yet. The biggest remaining work is mechanical integration, gearbox testing, and evaluating how the complete joint performs under load.

title: MSP430 Development Board
status: PCB complete; assembly and testing pending
tools: KiCad · PCB Design · Schematic Capture · Soldering
description: A custom MSP430 development board I designed from schematic through PCB layout, with assembly and hardware testing still to come.
overview: I designed this MSP430 development board as part of my PCB design coursework at NC State. The goal was to make a real, manufacturable board rather than just simulate a circuit. I worked through schematic design, component selection, layout, and getting the PCB manufactured. The board design is complete, but I still need to finish assembly and verify it on the bench.
technical: I created the schematic and PCB layout in KiCad, including component footprints, signal routing, power connections, and the physical layout of the board. I went through the process of preparing the design for fabrication and having the board manufactured. This project gave me hands-on experience with the practical details of designing a PCB that can actually be built.
decisions: I treated this as a complete board-design exercise, paying attention to physical layout and manufacturability rather than stopping once the schematic was electrically connected. I also wanted a board I could solder and test myself so I could follow the design all the way through to hardware.
challenges: The main completed milestone is the manufactured PCB. Assembly and electrical bring-up are still pending, so I’m not claiming it as a tested or fully working development board yet. The next part is checking the power and programming connections and verifying that the hardware operates as intended.

title: STM32 Bare Metal
description: Hands-on STM32 firmware experiments focused on understanding how microcontrollers work close to the hardware.
overview: I’ve been spending time working with STM32 microcontrollers outside of larger projects, focusing on the fundamentals of embedded firmware. The idea is to understand the hardware and peripheral behavior rather than treating everything as a black box. These are smaller experiments, not a finished product.
technical: My experiments include working with an STM32F103 Nucleo board and basic GPIO output, including driving LEDs. I’ve also used STM32 microcontrollers in larger firmware projects, which gives these smaller exercises some practical context. I’m keeping this page focused on the work I can directly show rather than listing every peripheral I’ve used elsewhere.
decisions: I’m using small, focused firmware exercises to get more comfortable with what the MCU is doing and how code interacts with hardware. They’re easier to debug and understand than trying to learn everything inside a full robot application.
challenges: The visible result so far is a simple hardware demonstration on the Nucleo board. I plan to document the actual source code and tests here as I organize them, rather than claim features that aren’t shown yet.

title: Autonomous / IoT Robot Car
description: An autonomous and IoT-connected robot car built for ECE 306 at NC State.
overview: This was a course project for ECE 306 involving a small robot car with autonomous and IoT functionality. It was an opportunity to apply embedded systems concepts to something that moves in the physical world instead of just testing code on a development board.
technical: The project combined embedded programming with a mobile robot platform. I’m keeping the technical details limited here until I’ve gone back through the project code and can accurately document the specific sensors, control logic, and communication features we implemented.
decisions: The project was developed within the requirements of ECE 306, so the design was shaped by the available hardware and course objectives.
challenges: The course project was completed. I still need to organize the original implementation details, photos, and results before giving a more thorough technical breakdown.

title: Sidekick Automation
tools: Customer Discovery · Robotics · Mechanical Design · Product Development
description: A senior design project exploring simple, reconfigurable benchtop automation for repetitive manual manufacturing tasks.
overview: Sidekick Automation is our engineering entrepreneurship senior design project at NC State. We’re investigating why repetitive manual tasks can be difficult to automate, especially in high-mix, low-volume manufacturing. Our current concept is a compact robotic arm that attaches to a workbench, can be taught without complicated programming, and works with interchangeable task-specific modules. We’re still early in development, so most of the work so far has been customer discovery and defining what the system actually needs to do.
technical: The concept we’re evaluating is a compact, approximately four-degree-of-freedom arm with a linkage-driven layout and actuators concentrated near the base. We’ve discussed hand-guided teaching, repeatable motion, and quick-connect modules that combine task-specific fixtures or tooling with the arm. A screwdriving setup, for example, would need more than a robot holding a screwdriver; it would also need a practical way to present screws and locate parts. These are design directions, not implemented or validated features yet.
decisions: Our interviews have repeatedly brought up the cost and difficulty of integration, changeovers, and adapting automation to different tasks. That’s why we’ve been focusing less on building a general-purpose industrial robot and more on the setup around a simple benchtop task. I’ve been leading much of our outreach to manufacturers, engineers, and automation specialists, including coordinating interviews and an industrial site visit, to make sure we’re solving a real problem before committing to hardware.
challenges: The biggest challenge so far has been narrowing a broad automation problem into something specific enough to prototype and test. We have an early concept and feedback from industry conversations, but we haven’t built or demonstrated the complete robotic system. Our next engineering work is to translate the findings into a constrained prototype and test whether the quick setup and modular approach actually help.
